opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the key distinction is between forecasting what *will* happen and forecasting what *would* happen if we took some particular action. Commercial incentives are actually pretty good at pushing on the first kind. If you can predict demand, prices, or what a user will click on, there's obviously money in that, and lots of very capable people are working on it.

Action-conditional forecasting is different. You're asking: if this government passed this policy, or if this lab adopted this safety practice, or if we coordinated on this treaty, how would the world look in five or ten years? The people who most need those answers are often the ones least able to pay for them, or the value is so diffuse that no single actor captures it. If I build a model that helps policymakers avoid a catastrophic mistake, the benefit goes to basically everyone, and I can't charge everyone. That's a classic public good.

There's also a worry about who gets this capability first. If powerful conditional forecasting is mostly developed inside a few companies, or by actors who want to optimize for their own narrow interests, it becomes a strategic advantage, a way to out-plan everyone else. I'd much rather the broad public, civil society, and democratic institutions have access to good tools for asking "what happens if we do X instead of Y?" That's part of how we keep human decision-making meaningful as AI systems get more capable. If only the most powerful actors can see the consequences of their choices clearly, that's a recipe for further concentration of power and for everyone else being sidelined.

And honestly, the technical problem is just underinvested. Causal and counterfactual questions are hard to evaluate. You often don't get to see the road not taken, so there's no clean feedback signal, and that makes it unattractive for a business that wants measurable metrics quickly. But that's exactly the kind of foundational work where a bit of careful, publicly minded research can move things a lot: building benchmarks, figuring out how to validate conditional predictions, and making sure the outputs are interpretable and trustworthy enough that people actually use them well.

So it's not that commercial forecasting is bad. It's that the part of the problem that matters most for navigating a world transformed by AI is precisely the part the market is least likely to provide on its own.

r001.rationale: The response describes forecasts of outcomes under specific policies or coordinated actions and explains that their broad, diffuse benefits make them difficult to fund commercially, calling this a public good.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the first thing to say is that I agree there are strong commercial incentives to build forecasting models in general. Hedge funds, insurance companies, ad platforms — they all want to predict what's going to happen, and they'll pay a lot for it. So you might think, why would anyone need to work on this as a public good? The market will take care of it.

But I think there's a distinction that matters a lot here, which is between forecasting what will happen and forecasting what would happen if we did X. The second one, the action-conditional version, is the thing that's actually useful for making decisions. If I'm a government deciding whether to pass some regulation, I don't just want to know what GDP will be next year. I want to know what GDP will be next year if I pass it versus if I don't. And that counterfactual question is just much harder, and it's also much less well served by commercial incentives.

Part of the reason is that the commercially valuable forecasts tend to be about things where you can trade on the answer, or where you're the one taking the action and you capture the benefit. A company can run an A/B test and figure out what happens if they change their button colour. But for the big collective decisions, like what happens if we adopt this AI governance regime, or this climate policy, nobody individually captures enough of the value to pay for the forecasting. It's a classic public good problem. Everyone benefits from knowing, but no one wants to foot the bill.

There's also a feedback problem. With ordinary forecasting, you make a prediction, time passes, you see whether you were right, and the models get better. With action-conditional forecasting, you only ever get to observe one branch. You passed the regulation or you didn't. So the counterfactual is never directly checked, and that means the usual market mechanisms for rewarding accuracy don't work very well. Prediction markets struggle with this too — you can set up conditional markets, but they're thin and they have all sorts of incentive problems where people can manipulate the condition.

And then there's the point about who benefits. If a powerful actor has really good action-conditional forecasts and nobody else does, that's a huge asymmetry. They can essentially steer the world while everyone else is flying blind. So I think there's a real argument that this capability should be broadly available, in the same way we'd want things like weather forecasting or epidemiological models to be public. Not because the private versions won't exist, but because the distribution of who has access matters a lot for how things go.

The last thing I'd say is that I think this becomes especially important with AI. As AI systems get more capable, a lot of the decisions about how to deploy them, how to govern them, what to allow, are going to be made under enormous uncertainty. And if we had good tools for asking "what happens if we do this?" and getting a calibrated answer, that would make those decisions so much better. It seems like one of the highest leverage things you could build, and I don't see anyone naturally incentivised to build it for the public. So I think it's worth working on even though it's hard and even though the commercial world is working on adjacent stuff.

r001.rationale: The response says forecasts of what would happen under collective choices such as regulation or climate policy are not well served by commercial incentives, and describes them as a public good because everyone benefits but no one wants to pay.

astra-6.text:
The distinction I’d make is between predicting what’s going to happen and predicting what would happen if we took different actions. A forecasting model might tell you that some crisis is likely. But what you really want to know is: what could we do about it? Which interventions would actually help?

There are certainly commercial incentives to build that capability. If you’re a company deciding where to build a factory, you’d pay for good forecasts conditional on that decision. But those incentives don’t necessarily give us forecasts of the consequences that matter to everyone else, or make those forecasts publicly available.

For a public policy decision, the benefits of getting it right can be spread across millions of people. Nobody individually has an incentive to pay for the whole analysis. And the organisation paying for it may prefer to ask, ‘How does this affect us?’ rather than, ‘How does this affect everyone?’

So the public good is having a shared, accessible way to compare the likely consequences of different choices, including the uncertainty. That’s harder than ordinary forecasting, because conditioning on an action isn’t automatically the same as understanding its causal effect. But even with those limitations, it seems valuable to help people reason about what to do, rather than just what to expect.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shared, accessible way to compare consequences of policy choices as a public good, and explains that diffuse benefits and limited incentives leave this analysis undersupplied.

sol-6.1.text:
The distinction I’d make is between predicting what’s going to happen and predicting what would happen if we took different actions. If you’re making a decision, it’s that second thing you really want. You want to ask, “If we adopt this policy, what happens? And if we adopt this other policy, what happens instead?”

There are clearly commercial incentives to build good forecasting models. But that doesn’t necessarily give you a system that helps the public compare possible decisions. A company might build something useful for its own trading or planning and keep the results private. And many of the decisions we care most about have effects on people who aren’t in a position to pay for that analysis.

There’s also a technical gap. A model that’s good at predicting what usually happens isn’t necessarily good at predicting the consequences of an intervention. You need to distinguish the effects of an action from the reasons people chose that action in the first place.

So the public good I’m interested in is making those comparisons available and credible: helping people understand which choices might lead to better outcomes, with uncertainty made explicit. Commercial progress could provide a lot of the underlying capability, but I wouldn’t assume it will automatically deliver that.

r001.rationale: The response identifies forecasts comparing outcomes under different policies or actions as a public good and explains they may be undersupplied because companies can keep results private and affected people may not be able to pay.
